tldr: By tackling the inference latency bottleneck of large Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models through a two-tiered setup—slow action proposals coupled with fast, reactive edits based on the latest observation—this method dramatically boosts success rates from 42% to 97% on dynamic manipulation tasks with just 10 minutes of online real-robot reinforcement learning.
hero_caption: The four dynamic real-world robot manipulation tasks evaluated in this work: dynamic object picking from a rotating turntable, ball balancing on a tilted plate, object passing from an arm undergoing random motion, and table soccer kicking past a moving defender. All require instantaneous reactions and dynamic control.
overview:
In modern robotics, fine-tuning large pretrained Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models using reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as an exciting path toward highly reliable robot deployment. However, due to their sheer scale, VLA models suffer from high inference latency. While the robot is busy computing its next action, time relentlessly marches on in the physical world. As a result, by the time the robot begins executing an action, the world has already changed relative to the initial camera observation. This distribution shift can cause the robot's policy to fail completely in fast-changing dynamic environments.

Prior studies explored asynchronous inference schemes, such as predicting future actions in the background, but these approaches have mostly relied on imitation learning. They lack mechanisms to leverage RL to push past the limits of pretrained demonstrations and achieve higher reliability. Furthermore, standard RL algorithms break down under latency because the temporal relationship between observations and actions is severely distorted.

To bridge this gap, the authors build on the prior RL framework EXPO-FT and introduce Real-Time EXPO-FT. The core idea is to temporally decouple slow, expressive action generation from fast, reactive action edits. A large VLA asynchronously proposes rough action candidates ahead of time using its strong behavior prior. Then, right before issuing commands to the robot, a lightweight edit policy inspects the latest camera frame captured at that exact moment, applies a rapid tweak, and executes the highest-value action.

Across all 10 simulation environments in the Kinetix benchmark, this approach outperforms even delay-free baselines. On four dynamic real-world manipulation tasks, it boosts the average success rate from 42% to 97% with just 10 minutes of online real-robot interaction data and zero human interventions during learning.
contributions: Proposed Real-Time EXPO-FT, the first systematic reinforcement learning fine-tuning framework for latency-prone, large VLA models that satisfies real-time control constraints.

Established an inference and learning architecture that preserves the Markov property under latency by decoupling slow action chunk generation by the VLA from fast action modifications by a lightweight edit policy conditioned on the latest observation.

Introduced a lightweight Critic technique that filters candidates in the initial noise space before full action decoding, substantially cutting Bellman update computational costs and boosting training efficiency.

Demonstrated outstanding sample efficiency on 10 Kinetix simulation environments and 4 dynamic real-world tasks, reaching an average 97% success rate with only 10 minutes of real-robot interaction data and no human intervention.

sections.heading: Too Big a Brain for a Fast Body? The Latency Bottleneck in VLAs
sections.summary: Large pretrained VLAs possess rich behavioral priors, but their computational weight induces inference latency, rendering observations stale by execution time. This paper introduces a reinforcement learning framework that operates directly under latency, achieving both high reliability and real-time responsiveness.
sections.details:
Recently, fine-tuning large pretrained Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models with reinforcement learning (RL) on real robots has shown great promise for achieving high reliability. However, the impressive expressiveness of modern VLAs comes at a price: large model scale. While a robot computes its next action, real-world time continues to elapse. By the time an action is produced from an image, the physical state in front of the robot has already moved on.

This discrepancy between observation and execution—a distribution shift caused by inference latency—severely degrades robot reliability in fast-paced tasks. Prior works explored asynchronous inference and methods like Real-Time Chunking (RTC), which inpaint future actions in the background while the current chunk is executing. Yet these techniques are rooted in imitation learning and lack mechanisms to use RL to exceed the capabilities of the pretraining data. Applying RL naively to actions generated from delayed observations fails to deliver the high reliability RL is supposed to provide.

This is the key breakthrough of the paper: the authors assign the large VLA the role of asynchronously proposing action chunks ahead of time, while delegating the immediate, real-time adjustments to a lightweight edit policy conditioned on the latest observation. Realized as Real-Time EXPO-FT, this design delivers dramatic performance leaps in both simulation and real-world experiments.

sections.heading: Lightweight RL, Generative VLAs, and Real-Time Inference: Where Three Trends Converge
sections.summary: The paper categorizes related work into three domains: deep RL for manipulation, RL fine-tuning for diffusion/flow-based VLAs, and real-time inference schemes. The authors tackle the unexplored challenge of sample-efficient RL for VLAs under real-time dynamic constraints.
sections.details:
To place this work in context, it helps to survey three major research trends:

### Deep Reinforcement Learning for Manipulation
The central bottleneck in real-world robot RL is sample efficiency—learning within minimal trials. Prior methods such as RLPD used lightweight Gaussian policies to minimize inference latency and maintain high control frequencies. However, their small capacity prevented them from leveraging the generalist priors found in large pretrained models.

### Reinforcement Learning for VLA Models
Modern VLAs rely on expressive generative backbones like Flow Matching and Diffusion models. Because standard continuous-action RL algorithms cannot be directly applied to them, specialized RL approaches have been actively developed. Off-policy RL methods are particularly popular due to their high sample efficiency. EXPO-FT, which this work builds on, is one such method. However, existing VLA RL techniques implicitly assume an idealized delay-free world, steering clear of real-time control constraints.

### Real-Time Inference for VLAs
To address VLA computational delays, researchers have explored system-level optimizations like custom kernels and speculative decoding, alongside algorithmic solutions like Real-Time Chunking (RTC), which inpaint subsequent actions alongside currently executing ones. Nevertheless, these remain confined to imitation learning. The core insight here is that modern RL mechanics—specifically value evaluation via Q-functions and policy editing—can unlock far superior performance compared to existing real-time imitation methods.

sections.heading: The Foundations: Control Under Delay and Action-Editing RL with EXPO-FT
sections.summary: A review of the relationship between control loops and model latency, delay-handling via Training-Time RTC, and the mechanics of EXPO and EXPO-FT. EXPO stabilizes RL by training a compact edit policy to apply additive tweaks rather than updating the base VLA weights directly.
sections.details:
Two foundational concepts are crucial for understanding this approach:

### Latency in Real-Time Control and Training-Time RTC
When a robot operates at control frequency $f$ Hz and VLA inference takes $t$ seconds, inference incurs a delay of approximately $d = \lfloor t \times f \rfloor + 1$ steps. Contemporary VLAs utilize Action Chunking: they predict an action sequence of horizon $H$ and execute the first $C$ steps. But if inference takes $d$ steps, the first $d$ steps of the newly generated chunk are already outdated by the time calculation finishes.

Training-Time RTC solves this within imitation learning by feeding the remaining action prefix of the ongoing chunk, $a^{\text{prev}}_{t:t+d}$, into the VLA as a fixed conditioning prefix. The VLA then predicts subsequent actions conditioned on this prefix, smoothly chaining actions together despite latency.

### How EXPO and EXPO-FT Work
EXPO is an algorithm designed to efficiently and stably train expressive generative models (such as flow policies) using RL. Its defining feature is that rather than updating the pretrained base VLA weights $\pi_{\text{VLA}}$ directly with Q-gradients, it introduces a compact edit policy $\pi_{\text{edit}}$.

The edit policy outputs a small bounded offset $\hat{a} \in [-\beta, \beta]$ on top of the base action $a$, yielding the final action $\tilde{a} = a + \hat{a}$. Backpropagating Q-value gradients solely through this edit policy makes training remarkably stable. EXPO-FT scales this recipe to VLA fine-tuning, but it did not account for inference latency.

sections.heading: The Proposed Method: Heavy Computation Ahead of Time, Quick Edits Right at Execution
sections.summary: The essence of Real-Time EXPO-FT is a two-tiered balance between slow VLA inference and fast action editing. The VLA asynchronously generates multiple candidate trajectories from older observations, and a lightweight policy conditioned on the latest frame refines them and selects the optimal action instantaneously.
sections.details:
### The Core Issue: Latency Breaks Reinforcement Learning
RL fundamentally assumes a Markov Decision Process (MDP), where an action $a_t$ is chosen based on the current state $s_t$. When an inference delay of $d$ steps occurs, the executed action depends on an older state $s_{t-d}$, making the process non-Markovian. This corrupts credit assignment—evaluating which action actually produced good outcomes—and severely degrades performance in precision-critical dynamic tasks.

### Two-Tiered Hybrid Inference
Real-Time EXPO-FT resolves this breakdown by separating two distinct timescales:

- **Asynchronous VLA Action Generation (Slow)**: When the currently executing chunk has $d$ steps remaining, the system takes the current observation $s_t$ and the executing prefix, and samples $N$ future action candidates from the VLA.
- **Synchronous Action Editing and Selection (Fast)**: The moment step $t+d$ arrives to begin executing the new chunk, the system acquires the **latest observation $s_{t+d}$**. A lightweight edit policy $\pi^{\text{edit}}_{\theta}$ rapidly applies subtle corrections to each candidate, and an action critic $Q_\phi$ deterministically picks the highest-value chunk evaluated under the fresh state to execute.

Because editing and selection happen with respect to $s_{t+d}$, the overall environment maintains a clean Markovian property despite the presence of latency—an exceptionally elegant design.

### Training Objectives and Noise-Level Filtering
During training, the base VLA is updated on successful trajectories using the Training-Time RTC loss, while the edit policy is trained to maximize Q-values.

However, decoding dozens of candidate trajectories through the full VLA during every Bellman update (target computation) incurs massive computational overhead. To overcome this, the authors introduce noise-level filtering using a lightweight critic $Q^{\text{dn}}_\psi$ that evaluates and filters candidates at the generative model's initial noise stage. This reduces full VLA decodings to just one per target computation while still retaining the high value-estimation accuracy of evaluating many candidates (e.g., 32).

sections.heading: Experimental Results: Success Soars from 42% to 97% in Just 10 Minutes
sections.summary: Evaluated across 10 physics simulation tasks and 4 dynamic real-world manipulation tasks, the method outperformed delay-free baselines in simulation and reached an average 97% success rate with just 10 minutes of online interaction on the physical robot.
sections.details:
### Simulation Experiments (Kinetix Benchmark)
The method was evaluated on 10 challenging physics tasks in Kinetix involving force control and disturbance noise. Under an enforced 4-step inference latency on the base policy, the proposed method achieved an average success rate of **96.2%**.

This significantly outpaced strong baselines under the same 4-step delay, including DSRL (61.7%), DSRL w/ RTC (76.1%), EXPO-FT (74.9%), and EXPO-FT w/ RTC (81.7%). Remarkably, it **even outperformed RLPD trained from scratch in an idealized setting with zero latency (81.4%)**. Combining the expressive prior of a pretrained model with instantaneous corrections based on the latest observation completely overcomes the penalty of latency.

### Real-Robot Experiments (4 Dynamic Tasks)
Using a physical robot arm running 30 Hz Cartesian velocity control, the authors evaluated four dynamic tasks:

- **Ball Balancing**: Keeping a ping-pong ball centered on a tilted plate; requires extreme reaction speed as tiny tilts accelerate the ball quickly.
- **Dynamic Picking**: Grasping a block moving on a rotating turntable.
- **Object Passing**: Snatching a spatula held by another arm undergoing random movements.
- **Soccer Kicking**: Kicking a ball into a small goal past a moving defender.

To simulate compute constraints, a latency of ~167 ms (5 steps) was injected (the dynamic picking task had an original latency of 67 ms / 3 steps). Capping online robot interaction data to just 10 minutes, the average policy success jumped from 42% (pretrained) to **97% (29/30 successes)** with Real-Time EXPO-FT. On ball balancing, which features high randomness, the proposed approach achieved 28/30 successes, while other methods peaked at 23/30.

In additional stress tests varying latency duration and object movement speeds, baseline policies degraded sharply, whereas Real-Time EXPO-FT maintained robust success rates throughout.

captions.F3: Comparison of training curves across all 10 Kinetix simulation tasks. Under a 4-step inference delay, Real-Time EXPO-FT (bold orange) outperforms all delayed baselines and surpasses even delay-free RLPD (thin blue), exhibiting outstanding learning speed and asymptotic performance.

sections.heading: Summary and Next Steps: Moving Toward Autonomous Resets and Generalist Rewards
sections.summary: Real-Time EXPO-FT unlocks real-time reinforcement learning for VLAs in dynamic environments. Remaining challenges include human intervention during physical environment resets and the need for task-specific reward detectors.
sections.details:
This work demonstrates that the fundamental real-world deployment bottleneck of VLA inference latency can be resolved through reinforcement learning and a smart temporal decoupling architecture. Adapting policies to dynamic, unpredictable real-world tasks to near-perfection with just 10 minutes of online data is an encouraging result for robotics researchers.

However, several limitations remain on the path toward fully autonomous learning:
- **Manual Environment Resets**: In these experiments, physical resets at the end of episodes (such as retrieving a dropped ball) partially relied on human operators, imposing an operational burden. Automating reset behaviors will be a key future step.
- **Task-Specific Success Detectors**: Sparse rewards were provided via hand-crafted, rule-based success detectors tailored to each task. Determining how to formulate reward designs that are universally robust for VLA RL fine-tuning remains an open question.

sections.heading: Appendix: Benefits of Noise-Level Filtering and Implementation Details
sections.summary: Details on the computational benefits of noise-level filtering for Bellman updates, along with network architectures, camera setups, and latency simulation parameters used in real-robot deployments.
sections.details:
### The Power of Noise-Level Filtering
Sampling many action candidates ($N=32$) during inference is vital for handling dynamic task uncertainty. However, decoding all 32 candidates through the full VLA during every training Bellman update would trigger a computational explosion. The appendix compares learning curves per compute budget between noise-level filtering ($Q_f$) and brute-force full decoding. For the same computational budget (PFLOPs), noise-level filtering reaches high success rates far more rapidly.

### Real-Robot System and Model Configurations
- **Base VLA**: Built on an OpenVLA-style $\pi_{0.5}$ base model, tuned with LoRA on Gemma 2B (language side) and Gemma 300M (action expert side). Input images are $224 \times 224$, the action chunk horizon is $H=16$, and execution length is $C=8$.
- **Critic and Edit Policy**: The critic employs a lightweight ResNetV2 (pre-activation) visual encoder within a 10-network REDQ ensemble. The edit policy is a compact 3-layer MLP (hidden dim 256) tanh Gaussian policy, operating at high speed by reusing image embeddings from the critic.
- **Rewards and Observations**: The setup avoids external sensors, detecting task success automatically using only images from the robot's wrist and external cameras alongside proprioceptive state.

takeaways: Temporally decoupling 'slow, coarse proposals from a large model' and 'fast, reactive last-moment adjustments from a small model' is an exceptionally powerful pattern for deploying heavy models into latency-sensitive physical settings.
When applying RL under latency, conditioning final action selection and value evaluation on the newest state preserves the Markov property and prevents training breakdown.

In generative RL (diffusion/flow policies), filtering candidates in the initial noise space rather than the decoded action space drastically lowers Bellman computation costs while preserving sample diversity.
limitations: Physical environment resets during experiments (e.g., retrieving dropped balls) still partially require human intervention; automated reset mechanics are needed for continuous 24/7 autonomous learning.
Sparse rewards currently depend on hand-crafted, rule-based success detectors per task; generalizing reward design is essential for rapid deployment to open-ended tasks.
On ultra-slow hardware where VLA inference delay $d$ exceeds the execution chunk length $C$, the core assumption ($d \leq C$) is violated and would require additional architectural adaptations.
